When vision-language models are fine-tuned for robotic action prediction, which representational changes are associated with training and which are inherited from the pretrained backbone?
We conduct a cross-architecture representational analysis of three Vision-Language-Action models across four LIBERO task suites, using layer-wise action probes, attention profiling, and counterfactual instruction perturbations to compare trained and reference checkpoints.
We find that VLM-to-VLA fine-tuning produces a consistent exit-layer collapse in action-probe decodability that is absent in VLA-to-VLA transitions and in NLP instruction-tuning controls, suggesting this reorganization is specific to action-oriented training.
Complementary analyses reveal that trained VLAs develop substantial sensitivity to instruction content while the dominant attention patterns at early layers largely pre-exist in pretrained backbones.
These findings provide a cross-architecture decomposition of instruction routing in fine-tuned VLAs, disentangling training-associated representational changes from inherited structure.

1	\section{Related Work}\label{sec:related_work}
2	
3	\paragraph{Vision-language-action models.}
4	VLAs fine-tune large language models on robot demonstrations to produce actions from visual and language input~\cite{brohan2023_rt2,kim2024_openvla,karamcheti2024,black2024_pi0,zheng2024tracevla,hung2025nora,xiao2025ava}.
5	NLP instruction tuning is well-characterized behaviorally~\cite{wei2022finetuned,ouyang2022training}, but the representational effects of VLA fine-tuning remain unexamined.
6	Fine-tuning operates in a low intrinsic dimension~\cite{aghajanyan2021intrinsic} and can distort pretrained features~\cite{kumar2022finetuning}; recent VLA-specific work proposes representation-preserving strategies~\cite{grover2025preserving,hancock2025actions}. Existing analyses target single architectures and cannot separate training dynamics from backbone artifacts.
7	
8	\paragraph{Mechanistic and behavioral analysis.}
9	Mechanistic interpretability has revealed residual stream communication~\cite{elhage2021}, induction heads~\cite{olsson2022}, and task circuits~\cite{wang2023_ioi,conmy2023}; causal tracing localizes factual recall~\cite{meng2022_rome}; attention probing shows heads encode syntactic relations~\cite{clark2019} and most can be pruned~\cite{michel2019sixteen}.
10	In VLMs, recent work characterizes visual token redundancy~\cite{fan2026visual}, progressive visual-textual alignment~\cite{neo2025interpreting,long2026understanding}, and instruction tokens as shallow-layer modality arbitration anchors~\cite{zhang2026instruction}.
11	Behavioral evaluations of VLAs reveal visual dominance~\cite{grant2026,hou2026,fei2025}; mechanistic studies identify sparse semantic directions~\cite{haon2025}, interpretable features~\cite{swann2026,buurmeijer2026}, symbolic representations~\cite{lu2025,molinari2025}, comprehension-action trade-offs~\cite{fang2025}, and task-specific attention heads for selective fine-tuning~\cite{mitra2025mechanistic}.
12	Concurrent continual-learning studies find that pretrained VLAs resist forgetting under sequential fine-tuning~\cite{liu2026forgetting}, consistent with our observation that VLA-to-VLA transitions preserve exit-layer structure.
13	All prior representational analyses target a single architecture; our $3 \times 4$ cross-architecture matrix tests whether mechanisms replicate across backbone families.
14	
15	\paragraph{Concurrent work.}
16	Fang et al.~\cite{fang2026when} construct a behavioral benchmark of counterfactual instruction failures on LIBERO; their evaluation measures \emph{whether} the model follows the correct instruction, while our perturbation measures \emph{how much} hidden-state geometry changes (\S\ref{sec:cf_sensitivity}).
17	Buurmeijer et al.~\cite{buurmeijer2026} probe low-level motor features in OpenVLA; instruction-level routing is the focus of our analysis.
18	Concurrent work addresses visual representation collapse~\cite{kachaev2025dont} and instruction information collapse~\cite{lian2026bayesianvla} during VLA fine-tuning; our $\Delta R^2$ metric offers a complementary diagnostic for measuring such collapse across architectures.
19	We additionally distinguish training-associated from inherited effects across three architectures, a decomposition absent from prior single-architecture studies.
20	
21	\paragraph{Probing and similarity methodology.}
22	RSA~\cite{kriegeskorte2008}, CKA~\cite{kornblith2019}, and linear probes~\cite{alain2017,belinkov2022} provide complementary geometric and functional evaluation.
23	We adopt RSA and MLP probes (CKA in appendix); the two metrics can diverge on the same data (Appendix~\ref{sec:cka_appendix}), and Cohen's $d$ vs.\ cosine distance are not comparable across trained/reference conditions (\S\ref{sec:cf_sensitivity}).

\section{Method}
\label{sec:method}

We investigate how action-relevant representations are organized across three VLA architectures using complementary probing, attention, and perturbation analyses.

%------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Architectures and Data}
\label{sec:arch_data}

We study three VLAs that span distinct backbone families (Table~\ref{tab:arch_overview}).
\textbf{OpenVLA}~\cite{kim2024_openvla,karamcheti2024} chains a frozen DinoSigLIP vision backbone~\cite{zhai2023_siglip,oquab2024_dinov2} (DINOv2 ViT-L/14 + SigLIP-SO400M), an MLP projector, and Llama-2-7B~\cite{touvron2023_llama2} (6.74B parameters, 32 layers, 32 multi-head attention [MHA] heads) for autoregressive 7-D action decoding.
It is pretrained on Open X-Embodiment~\cite{padalkar2023_oxe} (OXE; 970K episodes across multiple robot platforms).
\textbf{TracVLA}~\cite{zheng2024tracevla} pairs a SigLIP encoder with Phi-3-mini~\cite{abdin2024phi3} (3.8B parameters, 32 layers, 32 MHA heads).
TracVLA is trained on an OXE subset with spatial trace conditioning.
\textbf{NORA}~\cite{hung2025nora} uses Qwen2.5-VL-3B ($\sim$3B parameters, 36 layers, grouped-query attention [GQA] with 16 query heads and 2 KV heads) with the native Qwen2.5-VL vision encoder, which processes images at dynamic resolution without a separate projection stage.

Each architecture is evaluated in trained and reference conditions; we define the \emph{reference checkpoint} as the corresponding pretrained model before LIBERO fine-tuning.
A critical asymmetry distinguishes the reference baselines: the OpenVLA reference is an OXE-pretrained VLA, already fine-tuned for action prediction on 970K episodes, while the TracVLA and NORA references are pure vision-language models (Phi-3-Vision and Qwen2.5-VL) with no action training.
OpenVLA trained-vs-reference comparisons therefore measure a VLA-to-VLA transition; TracVLA and NORA comparisons measure VLM-to-VLA transitions.
For OpenVLA, two additional conditions support deep-dive analyses (\S\ref{sec:openvla_routing}): the Llama-2 base language model and a random-weight initialization.

We evaluate on LIBERO~\cite{liu2023_libero}, comprising four task suites (Goal, Spatial, Object, Long-Horizon) with 10 tasks and 50 demonstrations each.
The three architectures and four suites form a $3 \times 4$ matrix; 10 of 12 cells are filled (NORA Object and Long-Horizon lack available checkpoints).

Architecture details appear in Table~\ref{tab:arch_overview} (Appendix).

%------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Representation Extraction}
\label{sec:repr_extraction}

From each architecture, we extract hidden states at every transformer layer from two token positions: (a)~\textbf{image\_mean}, the mean activation over image tokens, and (b)~\textbf{readout}, the hidden state at the final pre-action token, which follows both image and instruction tokens in the causal sequence and can attend to all preceding context.
L0 denotes the embedding layer output, L1 through L$N$ the hidden states after each transformer layer ($N = 32$ for OpenVLA and TracVLA, $N = 36$ for NORA), with the final layer including the output layer norm.
In all three architectures, image tokens precede instruction tokens; the causal mask prevents image tokens from attending to instructions by construction.

We cross two factors in a $2 \times 2$ factorial design: \emph{training status} (trained vs.\ reference) and \emph{instruction presence} (with vs.\ without task description), applied to all 10 available cells in the cross-architecture matrix.
OpenVLA additionally provides representations from the DinoSigLIP projector output (4{,}096-D), DINOv2 and CLIP external baselines, and the branch-split before fusion; these sources support the OpenVLA deep-dive analyses (\S\ref{sec:openvla_routing}).

%------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Cross-Architecture Analyses}
\label{sec:cross_arch_analyses}

Three analyses are applied to every available cell in the $3 \times 4$ matrix.

\paragraph{Action probes.}
To quantify how much action-relevant structure is accessible at each layer, we train two-layer MLP probes~\cite{alain2017} to predict 7-DoF action vectors from frozen representations (architecture and training details in Appendix~\ref{sec:openvla_methods_appendix}).
We report probe $R^2$ as a measure of action decodability.
Higher $R^2$ indicates that actions are more accurately predictable from that representation under the probe; it should not be interpreted as evidence that the model causally uses that layer for action generation.
We define $\Delta R^2$ as the difference between the maximum layer-wise $R^2$ and the exit-layer $R^2$, and use $\Delta R^2 > 0.10$ as a descriptive threshold for substantial peak-to-exit reduction.
Train/test splits follow demonstration boundaries (demo-level splitting reduces $R^2$ from $0.7$--$0.9$ to $0.4$--$0.6$ vs.\ random splitting; Appendix~\ref{sec:delta_r2_threshold}).
95\% CIs are obtained via Monte Carlo cross-validation ($n = 1{,}000$ iterations) with demo-level resampling; the canonical peak layer is fixed from the full-data split to avoid winner's-curse bias.
Linear probes yield consistent patterns (Appendix~\ref{sec:linear_probe}).

\paragraph{L1 attention head profiling.}
To determine whether attention heads preferentially route instruction information to the readout position, each L1 head is classified as instruction-dominant ($>50\%$ of readout-token attention to instruction tokens) or image-dominant, reported as $k/N$ heads (32 for MHA, 16 for GQA).
Sensitivity analysis at thresholds from $30\%$ to $70\%$ confirms ordering robustness (Appendix~\ref{sec:threshold_sensitivity}).

\paragraph{Counterfactual instruction perturbation.}
To test whether the model's actions depend on instruction content, the instruction is replaced with four conditions: empty string, wrong task, shuffled tokens, and paraphrased.
We measure trained-model sensitivity via Cohen's $d$ on action MSE (OpenVLA, TracVLA) or cosine distance (NORA); reference VLMs use cosine distance on hidden representations.
These metrics operate on different scales; cross-metric ratios are invalid (\S\ref{sec:cf_sensitivity}).

OpenVLA additionally supports cross-instruction probes, representational similarity analysis (RSA)~\cite{kriegeskorte2008}, and external baselines (DINOv2~\cite{oquab2024_dinov2}, CLIP~\cite{radford2021_clip}); these single-architecture methods are detailed in Appendix~\ref{sec:openvla_methods_appendix}.

3	\label{sec:discussion}
4	\vspace{-4pt}
5	
6	\paragraph{Scope and limitations.}\looseness=-1
7	All findings are correlational (confounded by data distribution and optimization; $N = 2$ VLM-to-VLA transitions; Appendix~\ref{sec:claim_evidence_appendix}); we analyze causal-decoder VLAs on LIBERO only (flow-matching~\cite{black2024_pi0} and diffusion~\cite{ghosh2024_octo} architectures may differ); all analyses are open-loop.

docs/paper/experiments.tex:29:Counterfactual perturbation produces graded action divergence ordered by semantic distance ($d = 0.81$--$1.18$), and dose-response ablation of instruction-dominant heads yields monotonic trajectory divergence ($d = 0.48$--$0.64$; Appendix~\ref{sec:action_trajectory}).
docs/paper/experiments.tex:38:We define $R^2$ exit collapse as $\Delta R^2 = R^2_{\text{peak}} - R^2_{\text{exit}}$, the drop in action-probe decodability from peak layer to exit layer (Table~\ref{tab:cross_arch_matrix}).
docs/paper/experiments.tex:39:VLM-to-VLA fine-tuning is associated with substantial exit collapse across all tested conditions: TracVLA~\cite{zheng2024tracevla} $\Delta R^2 = 0.156$--$0.362$ across all four suites, and NORA~\cite{hung2025nora} $\Delta R^2 = 0.308$ (Spatial) and $0.455$ (Goal) (Figure~\ref{fig:r2_collapse}), all exceeding the $\Delta R^2 > 0.10$ threshold for substantive collapse (\S\ref{sec:cross_arch_analyses}).
docs/paper/experiments.tex:41:The gap between the largest non-collapse value ($0.097$) and smallest collapse value ($0.156$) spans $0.059$; any threshold in this interval yields identical grouping, and a permutation test rejects random label assignment ($p = 0.008$; Appendix~\ref{sec:delta_r2_threshold}).
docs/paper/experiments.tex:42:Even excluding NORA-Goal (whose bootstrap CI is unreliable; Table~\ref{tab:cross_arch_matrix}, footnote $b$), the VLM-to-VLA range remains $\Delta R^2 = 0.156$--$0.362$ (TracVLA only), consistently exceeding the $0.10$ threshold.

docs/paper/experiments.tex:155:If VLA training drove L1 instruction routing, reference models should show low counts that increase after training, as in OpenVLA's random-weight condition (0/32; \S\ref{sec:openvla_routing}); instead, both reference VLMs already saturate or near-saturate, and training leaves counts unchanged or slightly reduced.
